title: Perform inferential statistical tests to support group comparisons
when_to_use: When comparing group means or ranking groups (e.g., across categories, risk levels) to draw conclusions.
experience:
- For comparing more than two groups (e.g., project types, risk levels), run an ANOVA if assumptions (normality, homogeneity of variance) are met; otherwise, use the Kruskal-Wallis test.
- If the omnibus test is significant (p < 0.05), conduct post-hoc pairwise comparisons (e.g., Tukey's HSD, Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction) to identify which specific groups differ.
- For each pairwise comparison, report p-value, confidence interval, and effect size (e.g., Cohen's d, Hedge's g) to quantify the magnitude of the difference.
- Do not rely solely on descriptive ranking of group means; always accompany ranking with statistical evidence.
common_failure_prevented: Stating an order relationship (e.g., Medium > High > Low) without statistical evidence, leading to unsubstantiated conclusions.

title: Build a multivariable regression model before reporting single-factor trends
when_to_use: When exploring how multiple factors (e.g., team size, risk, satisfaction) relate to an outcome variable (e.g., cost deviation).
experience:
- Before reporting simple correlations, specify a regression model (e.g., linear regression) that includes all relevant predictors simultaneously.
- Check for multicollinearity (VIF > 5 or 10) and address it (e.g., remove collinear variables, use regularization).
- Report model coefficients, standard errors, p-values, and R-squared, interpreting each predictor's effect holding others constant.
- Compare the multivariable model's insights with simple bivariate relationships to identify if apparent correlations are spurious or confounded.
checklist: Specify regression model with all predictors
common_failure_prevented: Reporting only bivariate correlations without controlling for other variables, missing confounded or spurious relationships.

title: Use formal outlier detection and distribution shape metrics for descriptive analysis
when_to_use: When describing the distribution of a metric (e.g., cost deviation) across groups or overall.
experience:
- Beyond mean/median/std, compute skewness and kurtosis (or use |mean−median|/std) to quantify distribution shape. Use thresholds (e.g., |skew| > 1) to label as skewed.
- Identify outliers using the IQR rule (Q1 – 1.5*IQR, Q3 + 1.5*IQR) and list them, noting their impact on summary statistics.
- For each group, report the 95% confidence interval for the mean (using t-distribution) to indicate estimation uncertainty.
- If distribution is highly skewed, consider reporting median and IQR as primary statistics instead of mean/std.
checklist: Choose appropriate summary stats for skewed data
common_failure_prevented: Providing only basic statistics (mean, median, std) without formal outlier detection, shape quantification, or confidence intervals.
